Most Popular Narrative: 1% Undervalued

On the latest view, the narrative fair value of Arista Networks at $169.91 sits only slightly above the last close of $167.62. That small gap puts the focus squarely on how sustainable the current AI buildout looks rather than on any big pricing mismatch.

Arista reported Q3 revenue of $3.66 billion, up 58.5%, and forecast Q4 revenue between $3.9 billion and $4 billion. The headline is strong. One table in the 10-Q adds a detail worth holding next to it. Deferred revenue fell in the quarter, from $6,865.9 million to $6,839.5 million. A year earlier it rose $624.5 million. Revenue recognized from the opening deferred balance was $1,715.0 million, about 47% of Q3 revenue, against $699.7 million, about 30%, in Q3 2025. That balance holds multi-year support contracts and product deferrals tied to acceptance clauses. When large customers accept deployments, revenue comes out of it, so part of Q3's growth likely came from earlier shipments clearing rather than only from new orders. New deferrals were still $1,688.6 million, up from $1,324.2 million a year earlier. The balance is being refilled, just not faster than it's being drawn down. The CFO warned against reading one quarter too closely: "the deferred balance can move significantly on a quarterly basis, independent of underlying business drivers." I agree, and this isn't a bear case. Management's first look at 2027 is 38% to 40% growth, to about $18.5 billion. Arista expects $8.6 billion of revenue from remaining performance obligations, about 91% of it within two years, and purchase commitments rose to $11.4 billion from $9.7 billion in Q2. What I'd watch in the Q4 report is whether the balance grows again. If it does alongside revenue of $3.9 billion or more, demand is outrunning acceptances. If it falls again, growth is leaning harder on the balance, and the 2027 range carries more of the story. The Q3 call and both filings are here. One bullish story saw a fair value of US$209, a rough estimate of what the stock might be worth if AI demand kept driving 26.8% revenue growth with profit margins reaching 55.7% and a future P/E of 35.2x.

The more cautious view put fair value closer to US$153, assuming even faster 34.9% top-line expansion and 55.8% margins but arguing that a future P/E of 34.0x left little room for geopolitical or custom-ASIC risk.

What The Nvidia Evidence Did To The Argument

Nvidia’s Q3 2027 report showed revenue of US$115,844m and net income of US$65,287m, with net margin edging up to 56.4%. That profitability profile sat in the zone the optimistic case pictured for strong earnings power supporting a premium P/E, even as later leadership turmoil and governance concerns gave the cautious camp fresh material on key person and geopolitical risk.

The useful takeaway is clear. When a story leans on rich multiples, track whether margins and absolute profit, not just sales, move toward the scenario that was assumed. Then decide how much governance and concentration risk to price in.

Nvidia shares are about US$126 today, after a year to date decline of 33.4% from US$186. The analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St sees its Fair Value above that level, tied to a view that AI infrastructure buildouts and full stack AI factory offerings still underpin the business case.

As AI workloads expand, appetite for bandwidth and storage can influence how much practical computing customers actually obtain from Nvidia hardware. That tension could matter more as deployments deepen and spread.
